Title: Learning trajectories of children with special health care needs across the severity spectrum.

Journal/Date: Academic pediatrics (2015)

MeSH Keywords: Achievement, Australia, Child Health Services, Child, Preschool, Chronic Disease, Children with Disabilities, Female, Hearing Loss


--- ABSTRACT ---
[OBJECTIVE]: A significant proportion of school-aged children experience special health care needs (SCHN) and seek care from pediatricians with a wide range of condition types and severity levels. This study examines the learning pathways of children with established (already diagnosed at school entry) and emerging (teacher identified) SHCN from school entry through the elementary school years.
[METHODS]: The Longitudinal Study of Australian Children (LSAC) is a nationally representative clustered cross-sequential sample of 2 cohorts of Australian children which commenced in May 2004. Data were analyzed from the LSAC kindergarten cohort (n = 4,983), as well as a subsample of 720 children for whom teachers also completed the Australian Early Development Index checklist, a measure of early childhood development at school entry that includes SHCN.
[RESULTS]: Latent class analysis was utilized to establish 3 academic trajectories from 4-5 to 10-11 years: high (24.3%), average (49.8%), and low (23.6%). Descriptive statistics revealed a trend for both children with established and emerging SHCN to fall into weaker performing learning pathways. Multinomial logistic regression focusing on those children with emerging SHCN confirmed this pattern of results, even after adjustment for covariates (relative risk 3.06, 95% confidence interval 1.03-9.10). Children who additionally had low socioeconomic standing were particularly at risk.
[CONCLUSIONS]: Even children with less complex SCHN are at risk for academic failure. Early identification, together with integrated health and educational support, may promote stronger pathways of educational attainment for these children. Achieving these better outcomes will require the involvement of both educational and health practitioners.

In general, a severe condition impacts GPA scores more negatively than a less severe condition. This applied to both disabled and typically developing peers, except children with autism and epilepsy, among whom buffering due to the parent's education did not seem to apply.

Title: School absenteeism in children with special health care needs. Results from the prospective cohort study ikidS.

Journal/Date: PloS one (2023)

MeSH Keywords: Female, Humans, Child, Male, Absenteeism, Prospective Studies, Schools, Academic Success


--- ABSTRACT ---
[OBJECTIVE]: Children with special health care needs (SHCN) due to a chronic health condition perform more poorly at school compared to their classmates. There is still little knowledge on the causal pathways and which factors could be targeted by interventions. We, therefore, investigated school absenteeism in children with SHCN compared to their peers.
[METHODS]: This study was based on data from the German population-based prospective cohort study ikidS (German for: I will start school). Children with SHCN were identified by the Children with Special Health Care Needs screener that captures five consequences of physical or mental chronic health conditions: (1) use or need of prescription medication, (2) above average use or need of medical, mental health, or educational services, (3) functional limitations compared with others of the same age, (4) use or need of specialized therapies, and (5) treatment or counseling for emotional, behavioral, or developmental problems. School absenteeism was defined as days absent from school due to illness during first grade and was reported by classroom teachers. Associations between SHCN consequences and school absenteeism were investigated by negative binomial regression models. Effect estimates were adjusted for confounding variables identified by a causal framework and directed acyclic graphs.
[RESULTS]: 1,921 children (mean age at follow-up 7.3 years, standard deviation 0.3; 49% females) were included; of these, 14% had SHCN. Compared to their classmates, children with SHCN had more days absent (adjusted rate ratio: 1.37; 95% confidence interval 1.16, 1.62). The effect was strongest among children with i) functional limitations, ii) treatment or counseling for emotional, behavioral, or developmental problems, and iii) those who experienced two or more SHCN consequences.
[CONCLUSIONS]: Children with SHCN have higher school absenteeism, which could-at least partly-explain their poorer school performance and lower educational attainment. SHCN-specific targeted interventions may reduce the adverse effects of SHCN on educational outcomes in children.

Children with established or emerging SHCN were more likely to follow weaker pathways; among children with emerging SHCN, adjusted multinomial regression showed about threefold higher relative risk of a weaker trajectory (RR 3.06, 95% CI 1.03–9.10). The paper explicitly notes risk even among less-complex SHCN, supporting an overall severity/complexity gradient, although the abstract does not provide separate mild/moderate/severe effect estimates. PMID: 25441651.

source_tools.relevance: Full abstract with sample, ages, repeated trajectory classes, effect estimate, and complexity interpretation

key_findings.finding: Longitudinal repeated-outcome evidence using a functional/health-needs definition: In the Infant Health and Development Program, 576 preterm/LBW children (median gestational age 33 weeks; birth weight mean 1,798 g) had Woodcock–Johnson math and reading measured at ages 8 and 18. SHCN was defined by prescription medication/medical-service use, special therapies, or any functional limitation; 80% met SHCN criteria. Math declined from 97.5 at age 8 to 90.1 at 18, and reading from 99.0 to 96.8; scores differed significantly between SHCN and non-SHCN groups for both subjects. This supports poorer achievement trajectories with greater health burden, but it is a binary SHCN comparison rather than an explicit graded severity analysis. PMID: 26724181.

source_tools.relevance: Abstract gives repeated ages, sample, SHCN/functional limitation definition, outcome means, and direction

key_findings.finding: Strong explicit severity-stratified educational evidence, but not repeated trajectory measurement: Norwegian registry data included 247,120 students aged 15–16 years with GPA. Diagnoses included physical, neurological, and neurodevelopmental disabilities, with condition severity recorded. Neurological/neurodevelopmental disabilities were associated with lower GPA, whereas asthma and diabetes had comparable GPA to peers; effects were most evident for ADHD/autism and notable for epilepsy. Across conditions, severe disability was more negatively associated with GPA than less severe disability. This is a graded severity relationship with substantial condition-specific heterogeneity, but the reported outcome is a single lower-secondary GPA rather than repeated outcomes over time. PMID: 37554667.

source_tools.relevance: Abstract explicitly reports severity comparison, sample/age, diagnosis-specific heterogeneity, and effect direction

key_findings.finding: Prospective repeated SHCN ascertainment with school outcome: German ikidS cohort data (n=751; third-grade age 8–9) assessed SHCN before school entry, end of first grade, and end of third grade. Ever-SHCN was associated with worse average German/math/science grade (adjusted mean difference 0.17, 95% CI 0.06–0.28; higher grade means poorer performance); third-year SHCN difference was 0.29 (0.16–0.41), and emerging and persistent SHCN were associated with poorer grades (0.31 and 0.25, respectively). This demonstrates timing/persistence-related heterogeneity, but does not provide mild/moderate/severe strata. PMID: 39631793.

source_tools.relevance: Abstract gives prospective repeated SHCN measurement, sample/age, outcome and estimates by timing/persistence

key_findings.finding: A prospective German cohort analysis (n=1,921; mean follow-up age 7.3 years) found SHCN children had more illness-related absence than classmates (adjusted rate ratio 1.37, 95% CI 1.16–1.62). The strongest absenteeism associations were for functional limitations, emotional/behavioral/developmental treatment or counseling, and having at least two SHCN consequences. This supplies an explicit burden/number-of-needs gradient plausibly relevant to school functioning, but it did not repeat academic achievement outcomes directly. PMID: 37352302.

source_tools.relevance: Abstract gives functional limitation and number-of-consequences strata, sample/age, and effect direction/estimate

key_findings.finding: Condition-specific longitudinally linked evidence is weaker for severity: a Welsh population linkage study identified 150 children with cystic fibrosis born 2000–2015, with 119 having age-10–11 KS2 results. Expected attainment was 77% English, 81% mathematics, and 82% science versus higher general-population ranges; hospital admissions in the assessment year were examined as a severity/absence marker, but no statistically significant attainment difference was found between the full CF sample and those without CF-related admissions. This suggests heterogeneity and insufficient evidence for a simple severity gradient in CF. PMID: 35909577.
